questions.explanation_text: The wrong statements are II and III . For magnetic substances, remember these NCERT-based facts: Diamagnetic substances have small negative susceptibility: $-1 \le \chi<0$ So statement I is correct. Paramagnetic substances have small positive susceptibility: $0<\chi≪1$ They do not have $\chi≫1$ . So statement II is wrong. Ferromagnetic substances have very large positive susceptibility: $\chi≫1$ They do not have $\chi≪1$ . So statement III is wrong.   • Paramagnetic substances have small positive susceptibility:

    $0<\chi≪1$

    So statement II is wrong.

  • Ferromagnetic substances have very large positive susceptibility:

    $\chi≫1$

    They do not have $\chi≪1$ .

    So statement III is wrong.

  • For ferromagnetic substances, relative permeability is also very large:

    $\mu_{r}≫1$

    So statement IV is correct.

$\text{II and III}$

Correct option: Option C.

questions.explanation_text: Magnetic hysteresis is exhibited by ferromagnetic materials. In ferromagnetism, materials like iron and cobalt show hysteresis when subjected to an external magnetic field. The process involves the alignment of magnetic domains in response to the applied field and retains a certain level of magnetization even when the field is removed. This characteristic behavior, which results from the energy loss in the system, manifests as a lag between changes in magnetization and the external magnetic field, forming a hysteresis loop. Therefore, the correct choice is: Option C : Only ferro

questions.question_html: A magnetic needle has a magnetic moment of $5 \times 10^{-2}Am^{2}$ and moment of inertia $8 \times 10^{-6}kgm^{2}$ . It has a period of oscillation of $2s$ in a magnetic field $B$ . The magnitude of magnetic field is approximately?
questions.explanation_text: Given, Magnetic moment, $m=5 \times 10^{-2}Am^{2}$ Moment of inertia, $I=8 \times 10^{-6}kgm^{2}$ Period of oscillation, $T=2s$ Since, $T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{mB}},T^{2}=4\pi^{2}\frac{I}{mB}$ $\Rightarrow B=\frac{4\pi^{2}I}{T^{2}m}=\frac{4 \times (3.14)^{2} \times 8 \times 10^{-6}}{2 \times 2 \times 5 \times 10^{-2}}=16 \times 10^{-4}T$ Hence, no option is correct.
questions.explanation_html:
Given, Magnetic moment, $m=5 \times 10^{-2}Am^{2}$

Moment of inertia, $I=8 \times 10^{-6}kgm^{2}$

Period of oscillation, $T=2s$

Since, $T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{mB}},T^{2}=4\pi^{2}\frac{I}{mB}$

$\Rightarrow B=\frac{4\pi^{2}I}{T^{2}m}=\frac{4 \times (3.14)^{2} \times 8 \times 10^{-6}}{2 \times 2 \times 5 \times 10^{-2}}=16 \times 10^{-4}T$

Hence, no option is correct.

questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: A jet plane having a wing-span of 25 m is travelling horizontally towards East with a speed of $3600km/hr$ . If the Earth's magnetic field at the location is $4 \times 10^{-4}T$ and the angle of dip is $30^{\circ}$ , then the potential difference between the ends of the wing is
questions.question_html: A jet plane having a wing-span of 25 m is travelling horizontally towards East with a speed of $3600km/hr$ . If the Earth's magnetic field at the location is $4 \times 10^{-4}T$ and the angle of dip is $30^{\circ}$ , then the potential difference between the ends of the wing is
questions.explanation_text: Let's work through the problem step-by-step: The plane's speed is given as 3600 km/hr. First, convert this speed into meters per second: $v=3600\text{km/hr}=\frac{3600 \times 1000\text{m}}{3600\text{s}}=1000\text{m/s}$ The Earth's magnetic field at the location is $B=4 \times 10^{-4}\text{T}.$ The dip angle is $30^{\circ},$ meaning the magnetic field makes an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. Hence, the vertical (downward) component of the magnetic field is: $B_{v}=Bsin(30^{\circ})=4 \times 10^{-4} \times \frac{1}{2}=2 \times 10^{-4}\text{T}.$ In such problems, the induced motional emf (electromotive force) for a conductor of length $L$ moving through a magnetic field is given by: $\epsilon=B_{⟂}vL,$ where $B_{⟂}$ is the component of the magnetic field perpendicular to the conductor. Here, the jet is traveling East, and it is typically assumed that the plane’s wings are oriented North-South. Therefore, only the vertical component $B_{v}$ contributes to the potential difference across the wings. Using the values: $v=1000\text{m/s}$ $L=25\text{m}$ $B_{v}=2 \times 10^{-4}\text{T},$ The induced emf is: $\epsilon=vLB_{v}=1000 \times 25 \times 2 \times 10^{-4}\text{V}.$ Compute the value: First, multiply $1000 \times 25=25000.$ Then, multiply $25000 \times 2 \times 10^{-4}=25000 \times 0.0002=5\text{V}.$ Thus, the potential difference between the ends of the wing is $5\text{V},$ which corresponds to Option B.
questions.explanation_html:
Let's work through the problem step-by-step:

The plane's speed is given as 3600 km/hr. First, convert this speed into meters per second:

$v=3600\text{km/hr}=\frac{3600 \times 1000\text{m}}{3600\text{s}}=1000\text{m/s}$

The Earth's magnetic field at the location is $B=4 \times 10^{-4}\text{T}.$

The dip angle is $30^{\circ},$ meaning the magnetic field makes an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. Hence, the vertical (downward) component of the magnetic field is:

$B_{v}=Bsin(30^{\circ})=4 \times 10^{-4} \times \frac{1}{2}=2 \times 10^{-4}\text{T}.$

In such problems, the induced motional emf (electromotive force) for a conductor of length $L$ moving through a magnetic field is given by:

$\epsilon=B_{⟂}vL,$

where $B_{⟂}$ is the component of the magnetic field perpendicular to the conductor.

Here, the jet is traveling East, and it is typically assumed that the plane’s wings are oriented North-South. Therefore, only the vertical component $B_{v}$ contributes to the potential difference across the wings.

Using the values:

$v=1000\text{m/s}$

$L=25\text{m}$

$B_{v}=2 \times 10^{-4}\text{T},$

The induced emf is:

$\epsilon=vLB_{v}=1000 \times 25 \times 2 \times 10^{-4}\text{V}.$

Compute the value:

First, multiply $1000 \times 25=25000.$

Then, multiply $25000 \times 2 \times 10^{-4}=25000 \times 0.0002=5\text{V}.$

Thus, the potential difference between the ends of the wing is $5\text{V},$ which corresponds to Option B.

questions.explanation_text: Ferromagnetic substances have a very strong response to an applied magnetic field. The magnetic susceptibility (χ) is defined by $\chi=\frac{M}{H},$ where $M$ is the magnetization and $H$ is the applied magnetic field. In ferromagnets, even a small $H$ can produce a very large $M$ due to the alignment of magnetic domains. This is why the susceptibility is often much greater than 1. To summarize the options: Zero: Incorrect, because the material responds strongly. $>1$ : Although technically true, it doesn’t emphasize how large the value can be. $<1$ : Incorrect, as this would be more typical for diamagnets. $≫1$ : Correct, because it indicates the susceptibility is many times greater than 1. Thus, the correct answer is: Option D: $≫1$ .

Ferromagnetic substances have a very strong response to an applied magnetic field. The magnetic susceptibility (χ) is defined by

$\chi=\frac{M}{H},$

where $M$ is the magnetization and $H$ is the applied magnetic field. In ferromagnets, even a small $H$ can produce a very large $M$ due to the alignment of magnetic domains. This is why the susceptibility is often much greater than 1.

To summarize the options:

Zero: Incorrect, because the material responds strongly.

$>1$ : Although technically true, it doesn’t emphasize how large the value can be.

$<1$ : Incorrect, as this would be more typical for diamagnets.

$≫1$ : Correct, because it indicates the susceptibility is many times greater than 1.

Thus, the correct answer is:

Option D: $≫1$ .

questions.question_text: Which of the following properties is 'False' for a bar magnet?
questions.question_html: Which of the following properties is 'False' for a bar magnet?

options.label: A
options.html: It doesn't produce magnetic field.

options.label: B
options.text: Its like poles repel and unlike poles attract.
options.html: Its like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

options.label: C
options.html: Its poles cannot be separated.

options.label: D
options.text: It points in North-South direction when suspended.
options.html: It points in North-South direction when suspended.

questions.explanation_text: The false property is Option A. Here’s why: A bar magnet produces its own magnetic field. In fact, you can observe this magnetic field by the attraction and repulsion it exerts on other magnetic objects. Option B is true since like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Option C is true because if you break a bar magnet, each piece becomes a smaller magnet with its own north and south poles; you cannot isolate a single magnetic pole. Option D is true since a freely suspended bar magnet will align itself along the North-South direction due to Earth’s magnetic field. Thus, the statement "It doesn't produce magnetic field" (Option A) is false.
questions.explanation_html:
The false property is Option A.

Here’s why:

A bar magnet produces its own magnetic field. In fact, you can observe this magnetic field by the attraction and repulsion it exerts on other magnetic objects.

Option B is true since like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

Option C is true because if you break a bar magnet, each piece becomes a smaller magnet with its own north and south poles; you cannot isolate a single magnetic pole.

Option D is true since a freely suspended bar magnet will align itself along the North-South direction due to Earth’s magnetic field.

Thus, the statement "It doesn't produce magnetic field" (Option A) is false.
